findings.title: `fire_unit_until` cannot stop the unit early — the blocking `run()` defeats the whole mechanism
findings.description:
`fire_unit_until` is the centerpiece of the #22 fix: its docstring promises it "stops the unit once the line lands," and the slice rationale is that "a cutover that waits for the unit to END waits for days. It waits for the line it needs instead." But the body is:

```python
run(["mt-run", *mt_run_args], sudo=True, check=False, stream=True)   # line ~355
reached = wait_for_unit_or_line(unit, cursor, pattern)               # polls + stop_unit
```

`run()` is a synchronous `subprocess.run(...)` (cutover_common.py:70) — it blocks until the child exits. And the child, `sudo mt-run minute`, is not fire-and-forget: `deploy/mt-run`'s `start_and_stream` runs `systemctl start --no-block` and then `while is_running "${unit}"; do sleep 2; done` (mt-run:127-129), i.e. it blocks until the oneshot service finishes. `mt-minute-pass.service` is one full `run_minute_cycle` (trailing phase **plus** the unbounded backfill-until-quota). So `subprocess.run` does not return until the *entire* firing — trailing and backfill — is done, and only then does `wait_for_unit_or_line`/`stop_unit` get to run. By that point the unit is already inactive, so `stop_unit` is never called and the "the timers own the rest" behavior never happens.

Net effect in the normal (no Ctrl-C) path: `fire_unit_until` blocks for the full firing exactly like the old `fire_unit` did, so the bounding the slice exists to deliver is not delivered, and the docstrings/comments are false. The early-stop only actually fires in the Ctrl-C-detach case (mt-run exits 130 while the unit keeps running, so `subprocess.run` returns first) — the opposite of the stated design. Data verdicts are still correct (the journal is read after the unit ends), so this is a timing/feature bug rather than corruption — but it undermines the slice's stated purpose and should be fixed before the cutover is run. The fix requires a non-blocking start (e.g. `Popen`/detach mode for the mt-run call) so the poll loop can observe the still-running unit.

This is masked by the test: `TestBoundedFiringAndRecord._fire` in `test/unit/test_cutover_921.py` replaces `cutover_common.run` entirely with `_fake_run` (returns immediately), so the real blocking `subprocess.run` is never exercised. `test_the_minute_firing_stops_once_the_trailing_phase_completes` therefore passes against a simulation that does not exist in production.

findings.title: `cagg_freshness_for_session` re-implements the cagg catalog read, omitting the `-infinity` normalization
findings.description:
This probe reads `stats.last_successful_finish ... WHERE job.proc_name = 'policy_refresh_continuous_aggregate' AND job.hypertable_name = %s`. That is exactly the read `cagg_freshness._read_refresh_job`/`_JOB_SQL` already performs (`cagg_freshness.py:78-82`), which the codebase uses as the single well-tested way to resolve a cagg's refresh job. Re-implementing it here is a DRY violation, and the copy drops two safeguards the original deliberately carries:

- **The `-infinity` sentinel.** `cagg_freshness.py:68-72` documents that `last_successful_finish` is `'-infinity'` for a policy that has never completed a run, and that "psycopg cannot load that into a datetime — it raises DataError mid-fetch," which is why the helper wraps it in `nullif(..., '-infinity'::timestamptz)`. `cagg_freshness_for_session` selects the column raw and uses an *inner* `JOIN ... job_stats`, so a never-run policy that has a `job_stats` row with `-infinity` raises an unhandled `psycopg.DataError` out of `run_verify` → `main` (which only catches `RepairScanTimeout`), crashing `--verify` with a traceback instead of the clean `[WAIT]`/`[FAIL]` verdict. It is latent in the primary path (the prod policy has run for weeks), but the failure mode is exactly the "indeterminate ≠ clean pass" discipline the module elsewhere upholds.
- **No statement timeout.** Every sibling read sets a budget (`HEALTH_MINUTE_SESSION_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT` 30s in the mass read, `TRUNCATION_SCAN_TIMEOUT` 600s in `build_truncated_day_index`, `CAGG_FRESHNESS_PROBE_STATEMENT_TIMEOUT` 10s in the helper); this `max(created_at)` scan over the whole universe for the session-day runs unbounded.

Recommendation: resolve `last_refresh` through the existing freshness helper (or at minimum replicate the `nullif('-infinity')` + `LEFT JOIN` + timeout), rather than holding a second, weaker copy of the catalog read.

findings.title: `mt-run *` sudoers grant is wider than the file's stated "nothing wider" principle
findings.description: `Cmnd_Alias MT_RUN = /usr/local/bin/mt-run *` grants the `manta` operator user the full wrapper with arbitrary arguments as root. The wrapper has a passthrough branch (`run_production_mt`, mt-run:159-197) that execs `/opt/manta-trading/.venv/bin/mt "$@"` — so `sudo mt-run <anything>` runs the entire `mt` CLI as root, not just the pass-starting verbs the cutover scripts actually issue (`minute`, `daily`, `kalshi`). The file's header comment claims "Exactly the commands those scripts issue, nothing wider." The practical risk is bounded here — the operator already holds `MT_READ` (`cat /etc/manta-trading.env`, i.e. all prod credentials) and the full installer — so this is a tightening opportunity rather than a new secret-exposure, but the `*` is materially broader than the verbs needed and sits in tension with the file's own least-privilege framing.

findings.title: Per-chunk `fetch_session_bounds` query is wasted for bar-less outcomes
findings.description: In the chunk loop, `fetch_session_bounds` is opened and queried unconditionally, but `judge_chunk_by_sessions` returns immediately (early `if not bars`) when the response carried no bars. For `EMPTY` outcomes (HTTP 404 / empty body — common for newly listed or delisted symbols) this is a `trading_sessions` round trip whose result is discarded. Across ~13k active symbols in the trailing phase (and ~69 chunks/symbol in backfill) that is a non-trivial number of dead queries per cycle. Guarding the fetch with `if bars:` (or passing an empty-bounds shortcut) would remove it without changing the verdict logic.
